capabilities.title: Choose Ray Data vs Pandas/Dask/Spark
capabilities.summary: Decide when distributed streaming data processing is warranted versus a single-machine or SQL engine.

when: Processing large datasets (>100GB) for ML training
Need distributed data preprocessing across a cluster
Scaling data processing from a laptop to a cluster
avoid_when: Small data (<1GB) on a single machine — use Pandas
Tabular data with SQL-like operations — use Dask
Enterprise ETL / SQL queries — use Spark

steps: Estimate the dataset size and whether processing must span more than one machine.
If the data is <1GB and fits on a single machine, use Pandas instead of Ray Data.
If the workload is tabular with SQL-like operations, prefer Dask.
If it is enterprise ETL or SQL-query workload, prefer Spark.

Otherwise — for >100GB ML datasets, distributed preprocessing, batch inference, multi-modal loading, or laptop-to-cluster scaling — choose Ray Data for its streaming execution and GPU/framework integration.

capabilities.title: Transform data with vectorized map_batches
capabilities.summary: Apply a batched, vectorized function over a Ray Dataset, preferring map_batches over row-wise map.

when: Applying a transformation to every record of a Ray Dataset
Preprocessing, cleaning, tokenizing, or deriving features over columns
avoid_when: Per-row logic that cannot be vectorized — use ds.map(row_fn) instead

steps: Define a function that accepts a batch (dict of numpy arrays or pandas Series), adds/mutates columns, and returns the dict.
Call ds = ds.map_batches(fn, batch_size=N); execution stays lazy until the dataset is consumed.
Increase batch_size (e.g. 1000–10000) to speed up vectorized ops, balancing against per-task memory.
Fall back to ds.map(row_fn) only when a transform cannot be expressed over a batch.

validation: Iterate a few batches via ds.iter_batches() and confirm the new/derived column is present and correctly typed
Confirm map_batches runs without raising on a sample partition
expected_outcomes: map_batches is 10–100× faster than row-by-row map
Larger batch_size yields faster vectorized throughput

capabilities.title: Run GPU-accelerated batch transforms
capabilities.summary: Request a GPU per map_batches task to accelerate heavy per-batch compute such as image or audio preprocessing.

when: Heavy per-batch compute such as image or audio preprocessing
A GPU is available and CPU throughput is the bottleneck
avoid_when: Lightweight transforms where CPU is sufficient — requesting GPUs wastes accelerators

steps: In the batch function, move batch data to GPU (e.g. torch.tensor(batch[col]).cuda()), run the compute, then return CPU numpy arrays via .cpu().numpy().
Call ds.map_batches(fn, num_gpus=1, batch_size=64) to request one GPU per task.
Tune batch_size to fit GPU memory.

validation: Confirm the transform is scheduled with num_gpus=1 (does not error on missing GPU or silently fall back to CPU)
Verify returned arrays are host numpy (not left on device)
expected_outcomes: Image preprocessing throughput scales from ~1,000 images/sec (CPU) to ~5,000 (1 GPU) to ~18,000 (4 GPUs)

capabilities.title: Distributed batch inference over a dataset
capabilities.summary: Read data, run a model per-worker over GPU batches, and write predictions back to storage.

when: Running a trained model over a large dataset offline
Batch/offline inference over multi-modal or tabular inputs
avoid_when: Low-latency online/single-request serving — Ray Data batch inference is an offline pattern

steps: Wrap the model in a callable class: load the model once in __init__ (per worker), run predictions in __call__(batch), and return {'prediction': ...}.
Read the input with ds = ray.data.read_parquet(source).
Run predictions = ds.map_batches(BatchInference, batch_size=32, num_gpus=1); passing the class loads the model once per worker rather than per batch.
Persist results with predictions.write_parquet(output).

validation: Confirm predictions.write_parquet wrote output files to the target path
Spot-check a written batch has a 'prediction' entry per input row
expected_outcomes: The model is loaded once per worker, avoiding per-batch reload overhead

capabilities.title: Stream sharded Ray datasets into Ray Train
capabilities.summary: Feed distributed datasets to a TorchTrainer so each worker iterates its own shard without loading the full dataset.

when: Distributed training with Ray Train (TorchTrainer) over large datasets
Need per-worker dataset sharding and streaming during training
avoid_when: Single-machine training on data that fits in memory — a plain DataLoader is simpler

steps: Create datasets with ray.data.read_parquet for train (and val) splits.
Pass them via datasets={'train': train_ds, 'val': val_ds} to TorchTrainer with scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=N, use_gpu=...).
Inside train_func, call ray.train.get_dataset_shard('train') to obtain this worker's shard, then iterate train_ds.iter_batches(batch_size=...).
Call trainer.fit() to launch distributed training.
Optionally cache preprocessed data by writing it to Parquet first and reading it back during training.

validation: Confirm trainer.fit() returns a result without a dataset-shard KeyError
Verify each worker receives a non-empty batch stream from get_dataset_shard()
expected_outcomes: Preprocessing is distributed across the cluster and data is streamed rather than fully materialized in memory

capabilities.title: Stream and tune processing of larger-than-memory datasets
capabilities.summary: Process datasets bigger than memory via streaming iter_batches, and tune parallelism with repartition and batch_size.

when: Dataset is larger than available memory
Throughput/parallelism needs tuning on a multi-core cluster
avoid_when: Small datasets that already fit in memory — extra repartitioning/streaming adds overhead

steps: Read lazily (e.g. ray.data.read_parquet) and consume with `for batch in ds.iter_batches(batch_size=N)`; data is streamed, not fully materialized.
Set ds.repartition(K) to match cluster parallelism (e.g. K=100 blocks for a 100-core cluster).
Increase map_batches batch_size for faster vectorized ops, balancing against per-task memory.
Prefer Parquet for ML data; note that Images and Pandas outputs cannot be written back (write unsupported).

validation: Confirm full-dataset iteration completes without OOM
Confirm the block count after repartition(K) equals K
expected_outcomes: Processing 100GB scales from ~30 min (1 node / 16 cores) to ~8 min (4 nodes) to ~2 min (16 nodes)
